common_name: Showa-no-Sakae Camellia (Ruffled Soft Pink Spreading Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Showa-no-Sakae's low, willowy, spreading branches make it a natural choice for espalier, low hedging, or draping over a wall rather than an upright specimen planting.

directions: Showa-no-Sakae bears semi-double, ruffled flowers about 2 inches across in a soft, creamy pink deepening slightly toward the petal base, centered on a cluster of bright golden stamens. Unlike many upright sasanquas, it grows low and wide on willowy, arching branches, reaching only 3-4 feet tall while spreading 6-8 feet, making it one of the best sasanqua choices for espalier work, low informal hedges, or cascading over a low wall. Its Japanese name translates roughly to 'Glory of the Showa Era,' honoring the long twentieth-century reign of Emperor Showa. Bloom begins in fall and can continue sporadically into early spring, and the plant tolerates shearing well for gardeners wanting to keep its spread in check.

common_name: Stars 'n Stripes Camellia (White and Rose-Red Striped Single Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Stars 'n Stripes is grown primarily for its unusual striped flower color rather than flower size or fullness, so give it a visible spot near a path or entry.

directions: Stars 'n Stripes produces single flowers with 7 to 9 broad petals in white boldly striped and flecked with rose-red, an unusual, eye-catching color combination rarely seen among sasanqua cultivars, which typically run solid pink, white, or red. Bred by Nuccio's Nurseries in California and introduced in 1999, it grows into a medium, upright-spreading shrub reaching 5-8 feet tall, with the dark green, relatively small leaves typical of the sasanqua group. Bloom occurs early to midseason, from fall into early winter, ahead of many later-blooming sasanquas. Because individual flowers vary in how much striping they carry, no two blooms look quite identical, adding to its appeal as a conversation-piece specimen.

common_name: Egao Camellia (Large Deep Pink Semi-Double Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Egao grows more vigorously and upright than many sasanquas, so allow it room to develop into a large screening shrub.

directions: Egao ('smile' in Japanese) opens large, semi-double flowers packed with 16 to 20 petals in deep pink, shading even darker toward the base of the lower petals, around a tight column of pale-yellow-filamented stamens. It is more vigorous and upright-growing than most sasanqua cultivars, and is thought to carry some Camellia japonica ancestry, which likely explains its larger flower size and sturdier habit. Imported from Tereda, Japan by Nuccio's Nurseries around 1977, it blooms in midseason and works well as a tall screen or background shrub rather than a low foundation planting. Its full, ruffled flower form gives it more show presence than the many single or simple semi-double sasanquas it grows alongside.

common_name: Pink Snow Camellia (Lavender-Blushed Light Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Pink Snow sets an unusually heavy bud crop, so keep moisture consistent during bud development in late summer and fall to support the display.

directions: Pink Snow bears semi-double flowers roughly 3-4 inches across in a light pink softly touched with lavender, opening over a long fall display from October into December. New foliage emerges an attractive burgundy before maturing to the glossy dark green typical of the species, adding a second season of interest beyond the flowers. It arose as a chance seedling in Beaumont, Texas, and is noted among sasanqua cultivars for setting one of the heaviest flower bud loads of the group. The shrub grows slowly into an upright, medium to large specimen, making it a good long-term specimen or screening plant along the Gulf Coast.

common_name: The Czar Camellia (Large Light Crimson Semi-Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; The Czar is valued for reliable, heavy flowering even on relatively young plants, rewarding patience less than many large-flowered japonicas.

directions: The Czar carries large, semi-double flowers 5-6 inches across in a bright light crimson, with three to four rows of thick, richly veined petals that reflex back from a tall, prominent cylinder of yellow stamens. Selected from a chance seedling near Melbourne, Australia in 1913, it remains a benchmark heirloom japonica more than a century later for its combination of vivid color and reliable bloom. The shrub grows in a compact, erect, stocky habit compared with many sprawling japonicas, easing its use in narrower garden spaces or as a foundation planting. Bloom occurs in midseason, and the large stamen cluster at the flower's center gives it strong contrast and pollinator appeal compared with fully double cultivars.

common_name: Lady Loch Camellia (Cotton-Candy Pink Peony-Form Heirloom Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Lady Loch is markedly drought-tolerant once established compared with many camellias, but still benefits from supplemental water during its first two seasons.

directions: Lady Loch produces large, informal double to peony-form flowers in cotton-candy pink, deepening to darker pink veining through the petals and softening to a stippled white margin at the edges. One of the older, tried-and-true heirloom japonica cultivars still widely grown in Southern gardens, it flowers reliably in midseason on an upright, dense shrub that becomes quite large with age. Its dense evergreen habit and tolerance of considerable shade make it a dependable large specimen or screening plant for the back of a shaded bed. Once established, it tolerates dry spells better than many camellias, an asset during Gulf Coast summer droughts.

common_name: Finlandia Camellia (White Chimera with Pink-Striped Sports)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; because Finlandia is genetically unstable and often throws pink-striped sports, prune out reverted branches if a solid white flower effect is desired.

directions: Finlandia opens medium to large, semi-double white flowers with swirled, fluted petals surrounding a bright cluster of yellow stamens, blooming early to midseason. The cultivar is a genetic chimera and frequently produces flowers streaked or spotted with pink to red on the same plant, or even within the same bloom, giving individual specimens a variable, sometimes bicolor look from year to year. It grows in a relatively narrow, upright, compact habit compared with many spreading japonicas, making it useful where height is wanted without a wide footprint. A distinct sport, 'Finlandia Variegated,' shows the pink streaking more consistently and is sold as a separate, more predictably patterned cultivar.

common_name: Mrs. D.W. Davis Camellia (Enormous Pale Apricot-Pink Semi-Double Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Mrs. D.W. Davis grows quickly for a japonica and develops an open, somewhat leggy habit, so light structural pruning when young helps build a fuller shrub.

directions: Mrs. D.W. Davis bears enormous, semi-double, somewhat pendant flowers in a pale apricot-pink, among the largest bloom sizes found in the japonica group. Raised by D.W. Davis in Seffner, Florida from a seedling of 'Elizabeth Boardman' that first flowered in 1951, it went on to win the American Camellia Society's Illges Medal in 1955 and remains a respected Southern-bred heirloom. The shrub grows rapidly into an upright but open, eventually large specimen or small tree with big, glossy, dark green leaves. Flowering runs through the winter into spring in mild climates, with the huge, soft-colored blooms showing best when given some protection from wind that can bruise their large petals.

common_name: Nagasaki Camellia (Rose-Pink and White Marbled Heirloom Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Nagasaki grows slowly and spreads wider than it is tall, so give it room and be patient waiting for a mature specimen.

directions: Nagasaki, also known by the older name 'Mikenjaku,' bears large, semi-double flowers 4-5 inches across in rose pink patterned with white markings, giving each bloom a distinctive marbled look. A nineteenth-century Japanese heirloom, it blooms later than many japonicas, opening in mid-spring rather than the depths of winter, which helps it escape some cold-snap bud damage in marginal zones. Growth is slow and distinctly spreading rather than upright, so it works well as a wide, informal specimen or an unclipped low screen. Its late bloom timing pairs well in a mixed camellia planting alongside earlier sasanqua and japonica cultivars to extend the flowering season.

common_name: Pearl Maxwell Camellia (Formal Double Shell-Pink Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Pearl Maxwell's dense, compact growth and long bloom window make it a good choice for hedging or espalier as well as a single specimen.

directions: Pearl Maxwell produces perfectly formed, fully double flowers in soft shell pink, 4-5 inches wide, with the tightly imbricated petal arrangement prized in formal camellia exhibition classes. It blooms over an unusually long window, from midseason into late season, often carrying flowers from February into May in mild Southern climates. The shrub grows dense and compact with an upright-to-rounded habit and glossy rich-green foliage, making it tidier and more manageable than many larger, looser-growing japonicas. Its long bloom season and reliable formal-double flower form also make it a favorite for cut flowers and camellia show entries.

common_name: Elegans Supreme Camellia (Ruffled Wine-Red Anemone-Form Sport of Elegans)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; like its parent 'Elegans,' Elegans Supreme spreads wider than it grows tall, so allow generous width when siting it as a specimen or foundation shrub.

directions: Elegans Supreme is a bud sport of the antique cultivar 'Elegans' ('Chandleri Elegans'), bearing large anemone-form flowers in wine-red to rose-pink with heavily ruffled, deeply serrated petals surrounding a center packed with smaller petaloids and yellow stamens. Raised by W.F. Bray of Pensacola, Florida, it earned the American Camellia Society's Sewell Mutant Award in 1966 and was later inducted into the William E. Woodroof Camellia Hall of Fame in 1980, recognition of its lasting popularity among japonica growers. Like its parent, it grows in a dense, spreading habit wider than it is tall, and blooms in midseason to late season. The deep, ruffled color and full anemone form give it more drama than the softer pink of the original 'Elegans,' while retaining the same reliable vigor and shade tolerance.
